claim: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic.
source: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic, but understanding of their diet is still tenuous.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the abundance and diversity of enantiornithines during the Mesozoic era.

claim: Understanding of enantiornithine diet is still tenuous.
source: Enantiornithines were the dominant birds of the Mesozoic, but understanding of their diet is still tenuous.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by the limited number of studies cited.

claim: Bohaiornithidae are famous for their large size and powerfully built teeth and claws.
source: We introduce new data on the enantiornithine family Bohaiornithidae, famous for their large size and powerfully built teeth and claws.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing bohaiornithid morphology (Wang, 2014a).

claim: Bohaiornithids are more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds; Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores; Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders; and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
evidence: This is supported by the comparative analyses of body mass, jaw mechanics, FEA, and claw morphometrics presented in the manuscript.

claim: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds; Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores; Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders; and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
evidence: This is supported by mechanical advantage, FEA, and body mass data presented in the results sections.

claim: Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds; Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores; Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders; and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
evidence: This is supported by pedal morphometric data showing similarity to large raptors.

claim: Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds; Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores; Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders; and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
evidence: This is supported by FEA and mechanical advantage data presented in the results.

claim: Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
source: We find bohaiornithids to be more ecologically diverse than any other enantiornithine family: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis are similar to living plant-eating birds; Longusunguis resembles raptorial carnivores; Zhouornis is similar to both fruit-eating birds and generalist feeders; and Shenqiornis and Sulcavis plausibly ate fish, plants, or a mix of both.
evidence: This is supported by mechanical advantage and FEA data showing affinities with multiple diet groups.

claim: The ancestral enantiornithine bird was predicted to have been a generalist which ate a wide variety of foods.
source: We predict the ancestral enantiornithine bird to have been a generalist which ate a wide variety of foods.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction using body mass, mechanical advantage, FEA, and pedal morphometric data.

claim: More quantitative data from across the enantiornithine tree is needed to refine the prediction of ancestral diet.
source: However, more quantitative data from across the enantiornithine tree is needed to refine this prediction.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current dataset and the uncertainty in ancestral state reconstructions.

claim: By the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction.
source: By the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction, adding to the evidence that traits unique to crown birds cannot completely explain their ecological success.
evidence: This is supported by the diversity of diets identified in bohaiornithids and other enantiornithine families, combined with their Early Cretaceous age.

claim: Traits unique to crown birds cannot completely explain their ecological success.
source: By the Early Cretaceous, enantiornithine birds had diversified into a variety of ecological niches like crown birds after the K-Pg extinction, adding to the evidence that traits unique to crown birds cannot completely explain their ecological success.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that enantiornithines achieved similar ecological diversity without crown bird traits.

claim: The diet of most Mesozoic birds remains speculative.
source: However, dietary evolution in birds outside the crown is poorly understood, largely because the diet of most Mesozoic birds remains speculative (Miller and Pittman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and the limited number of quantitative dietary studies.

claim: Some recent studies have begun to elucidate the matter of Mesozoic bird diet.
source: Some recent studies have begun to elucidate this matter (O'Connor, 2019a; O'Connor and Zhou, 2020c; Miller et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2022; Marugán-Lobón and Chiappe, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent publications on Mesozoic bird diet.

claim: The most progress in understanding Mesozoic bird diet has been made among enantiornithines.
source: The most progress has been made among enantiornithines (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2023), the most abundant and speciose birds in the Cretaceous (Pittman, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent quantitative dietary studies of enantiornithines.

claim: Enantiornithines were the most abundant and speciose birds in the Cretaceous.
source: The most progress has been made among enantiornithines (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023; Clark et al., 2023), the most abundant and speciose birds in the Cretaceous (Pittman, 2020a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pittman, 2020a.

claim: Only 12 of the over 100 described enantiornithine species have been examined for diet.
source: This progress only amounts to an examination of 12 of the over 100 described enantiornithine species (Pittman, 2020a), though.
evidence: This is based on counting the species examined in cited dietary studies and comparing to the total number of described species.

claim: The limited examination of enantiornithine diet has limited large-scale examinations of their overall trophic diversity and diversification patterns.
source: This has limited any large-scale examinations of the overall trophic diversity of enantiornithines and the patterns in which they diversified.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the small sample size relative to total diversity.

claim: Bohaiornithidae is phylogenetically intermediate to previously studied enantiornithine families.
source: Ideally, the next step to answering these questions is to examine a large group of enantiornithines which are phylogenetically intermediate to the previously studied families. The enantiornithine family Bohaiornithidae (Figure 1, centre) fits both of these requirements, and thus serves as an ideal stepping stone to a large-scale understanding of enantiornithine ecology.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analyses cited in Table 1 showing bohaiornithids positioned between other major enantiornithine clades.

claim: Bohaiornithids have robust teeth.
source: Bohaiornithids are iconic among enantiornithines for their robust teeth, large claws, large size (Wang, 2014a), and iridescent colouration (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang, 2014a describing bohaiornithid morphology.

claim: Bohaiornithids have large claws.
source: Bohaiornithids are iconic among enantiornithines for their robust teeth, large claws, large size (Wang, 2014a), and iridescent colouration (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang, 2014a describing bohaiornithid morphology.

claim: Bohaiornithids have large body size.
source: Bohaiornithids are iconic among enantiornithines for their robust teeth, large claws, large size (Wang, 2014a), and iridescent colouration (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang, 2014a and body mass estimates in Table 3.

claim: Bohaiornithids have iridescent colouration.
source: Bohaiornithids are iconic among enantiornithines for their robust teeth, large claws, large size (Wang, 2014a), and iridescent colouration (Peteya et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peteya et al., 2017.

claim: Bohaiornithid robust teeth have led the clade to be interpreted as durophagous.
source: Their robust teeth have led the clade to be interpreted as durophagous (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhou et al., 2021), while their large claws and large body size lead to raptorial interpretations (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous interpretations of bohaiornithid diet.

claim: Bohaiornithid large claws and large body size lead to raptorial interpretations.
source: Their robust teeth have led the clade to be interpreted as durophagous (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhou et al., 2021), while their large claws and large body size lead to raptorial interpretations (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous interpretations of bohaiornithid ecology.

claim: Bohaiornithidae has a troubled taxonomic history.
source: Bohaiornithidae has a troubled taxonomic history, with authors proposing the clade actually represents an evolutionary grade (Chiappe et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022b) or at least a group in need of phylogenetic redefinition (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent phylogenetic studies questioning the monophyly or definition of Bohaiornithidae.

claim: Some authors propose Bohaiornithidae represents an evolutionary grade rather than a clade.
source: Bohaiornithidae has a troubled taxonomic history, with authors proposing the clade actually represents an evolutionary grade (Chiappe et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022b) or at least a group in need of phylogenetic redefinition (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chiappe et al., 2019 and Wang et al., 2022b.

claim: Some authors propose Bohaiornithidae is in need of phylogenetic redefinition.
source: Bohaiornithidae has a troubled taxonomic history, with authors proposing the clade actually represents an evolutionary grade (Chiappe et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2022b) or at least a group in need of phylogenetic redefinition (Liu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2022.

claim: The original six taxa referred to Bohaiornithidae have consistently resolved as closely related taxa across the literature.
source: But across the literature, the original six taxa referred to Bohaiornithidae (Bohaiornis, Longusunguis, Parabohaiornis, Shenqiornis, Sulcavis, and Zhouornis) (Wang, 2014a; Figure 2) have consistently resolved as closely related taxa (Table 1), so for the purposes of this work we will refer to this group as a clade (see 'Methods' for further justification).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic summary in Table 1 showing these taxa frequently grouping together.

claim: Bohaiornithidae is the most speciose family of enantiornithine birds with the inclusion of Beiguornis.
source: With the recently described Beiguornis (Wang, 2022a), Bohaiornithidae is the most speciose family of enantiornithine birds.
evidence: This is based on counting the number of species in Bohaiornithidae compared to other enantiornithine families.

claim: Body mass has a strong effect on birds' diets.
source: Size has a strong effect on birds' diets (Navalón et al., 2019; Pigot et al., 2020; Natale and Slater, 2022), so estimating the mass of extinct birds (Serrano et al., 2015) helps narrow dietary possibilities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the relationship between body size and diet in birds.

claim: Estimating the mass of extinct birds helps narrow dietary possibilities.
source: Size has a strong effect on birds' diets (Navalón et al., 2019; Pigot et al., 2020; Natale and Slater, 2022), so estimating the mass of extinct birds (Serrano et al., 2015) helps narrow dietary possibilities.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the established relationship between body size and diet.

claim: Mechanical advantage of the jaw looks at trade-offs between bite speed and force.
source: Most commonly, the functional index used in ecology is MA of the jaw, looking at trade-offs between bite speed and force (Stayton, 2006; Corbin et al., 2015; Adams et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using mechanical advantage to understand jaw function.

claim: Three versions of mechanical advantage are collected alongside three other functional indices in this study.
source: Herein three versions of MA are collected alongside three other functional indices which have previously discriminated animal diet (Miller and Pittman, 2021; Ma, 2020).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, supported by citations to previous applications.

claim: FEA is an engineering tool used to model forces acting on irregular structures.
source: FEA is an engineering tool used to model forces acting on irregular structures (Bathe, 2014).
evidence: This is a definition of FEA supported by citation to an engineering textbook.

claim: FEA is used to model bird jaws during a bite in this study.
source: Here it is used to model bird jaws during a bite.
evidence: This describes the application of FEA in the current study.

claim: If an FEA model experiences less strain under the same relative load as another model, its shape can withstand a greater force before failure.
source: If a model experiences less strain under the same relative load as another model, its shape can withstand a greater force before failure.
evidence: This is a principle of engineering mechanics applied to FEA interpretation.

claim: By maintaining a constant relative load for FEA models, models can be compared in terms of relative strength.
source: By maintaining a constant relative load for FEA models, models can be compared in terms of relative strength (Dumont et al., 2009; Bright, 2014).
evidence: This describes the comparative methodology used in FEA, supported by citations.

claim: Traditional morphometrics describes the shape of animal parts with measurements relevant to their ecological role.
source: TM describes the shape of animal parts with measurements relevant to their ecological role (Marcus, 1990).
evidence: This is a definition of traditional morphometrics supported by citation.

claim: Measurements of pedal ungual curvature and relative size can differentiate between non-raptorial and raptorial birds.
source: Here, measurements are taken of the curvature and relative size of pedal unguals which can differentiate between non-raptorial and raptorial birds (Csermely and Rossi, 2006; Fowler et al., 2009; Csermely et al., 2012; Cobb and Sellers, 2020) and, potentially, between specific types of raptorial behaviour (Miller et al., 2022; Fowler et al., 2009; Einoder and Richardson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the relationship between claw morphology and predatory behavior.

claim: Measurements of pedal ungual curvature and relative size can potentially differentiate between specific types of raptorial behaviour.
source: Here, measurements are taken of the curvature and relative size of pedal unguals which can differentiate between non-raptorial and raptorial birds (Csermely and Rossi, 2006; Fowler et al., 2009; Csermely et al., 2012; Cobb and Sellers, 2020) and, potentially, between specific types of raptorial behaviour (Miller et al., 2022; Fowler et al., 2009; Einoder and Richardson, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies examining claw morphology in different types of raptors.

claim: The framework used in this study expands on past works by including traditional morphometrics of the skull.
source: We expand the framework used in our past works (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023) by including traditional morphometrics of the skull.
evidence: This describes a methodological addition to previous studies by the authors.

claim: Skull traditional morphometrics were recently used successfully in reconstructing the diet of longipterygid enantiornithines.
source: This line of evidence was recently used successfully in reconstructing the diet of longipterygid enantiornithines (Clark et al., 2023), so we expect it to be useful here as well.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Clark et al., 2023 demonstrating the utility of skull morphometrics for diet reconstruction.

claim: The study incorporates extant data from Clark et al., 2023.
source: We incorporate the extant data from Clark et al., 2023, collect new data for bohaiornithids, and analyse the data with a modified version of their methodology.
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the skull morphometric analysis.

claim: The study uses alternate sources of body mass and diet data compared to Clark et al., 2023.
source: Notably, we use alternate sources of body mass and diet data and adjust the data in an attempt to remove the effects of body size.
evidence: This describes methodological differences from Clark et al., 2023.

claim: Comparative data is taken from nearly 200 extant birds.
source: These proxies are of little use without reference values, so comparative data is taken from nearly 200 extant birds (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023), including tinamous, flamingos, turacos, strisores, and songbirds, among others.
evidence: This describes the extant comparative dataset used in the study.

claim: The extant bird dataset includes tinamous, flamingos, turacos, strisores, and songbirds, among others.
source: These proxies are of little use without reference values, so comparative data is taken from nearly 200 extant birds (Miller et al., 2022; Miller et al., 2023), including tinamous, flamingos, turacos, strisores, and songbirds, among others.
evidence: This lists examples of the taxonomic diversity in the extant dataset.

claim: Extant bird diet categories are based on the EltonTraits 1.0 database.
source: These birds are also ecologically diverse, with diet categories based on the EltonTraits 1.0 database of bird diet (Wilman et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the source of diet classifications for extant birds.

claim: Claw shape is not expected to correlate with diet but the use of talons.
source: Claw shape is not expected to correlate with diet but the use of talons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of claw morphology based on previous studies.

claim: Raptorial birds are separated into raptors taking small prey and those hunting large prey based on feeding records.
source: We follow the classification of Miller et al., 2023 separating raptorial birds into raptors taking small prey (which can be completely encircled in the pes) and those hunting large prey (which cannot be encircled by the pes) based on feeding records in the Birds of the World database (Billerman, 2023).
evidence: This describes the classification scheme for raptorial birds used in the study.

claim: The bird database AVONET allows expansion of the mass and diet dataset to 8758 of the 9994 recognised species of birds.
source: With the recent publication of the bird database AVONET (Tobias et al., 2022), we are able to expand our dataset comparing mass and diet to 8758 of the 9994 recognised species of birds.
evidence: This describes the expanded dataset made possible by the AVONET database.

claim: The crop and gizzard play major roles in folivory and granivory for extant avians.
source: The crop and gizzard (i.e. ventriculus or gastric mill) play major roles in folivory and granivory for extant avians, serving as a site to process the tough plant matter during digestion (Dudley and Vermeij, 1992; Gionfriddo and Best, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of avian digestive physiology.

claim: Crops and gizzards have previously been inferred to be absent in Enantiornithes.
source: Crops and gizzards have previously been inferred to be absent in Enantiornithes (O'Connor and Zhou, 2020c), which could potentially be strong evidence against folivory or granivory in Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor and Zhou, 2020c.

claim: Most groups of herbivorous lizards have minimal postcranial digestive specialisation and instead orally process plants.
source: Most groups of herbivorous lizards have minimal postcranial digestive specialisation, and instead are able to orally process plants to a level where nutrients can be efficiently extracted (Cooper and Vitt, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cooper and Vitt, 2002 on lizard digestive physiology.

claim: Skinks and tegus retain conical dentition which is more robust than their carnivorous and omnivorous relatives.
source: Better analogues are skinks (Scincidae) and tegus (Teiidae), which retain conical dentition which is simply more robust than their carnivorous and omnivorous relatives (Melstrom, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Melstrom, 2017 on lizard tooth morphology.

claim: Bohaiornithids have some of the most robust teeth within Enantiornithes.
source: Bohaiornithids, notably, have some of the most robust teeth within Enantiornithes (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a describing bohaiornithid tooth morphology.

claim: Robust teeth in bohaiornithids may have been an adaptation or exaptation for processing plant matter.
source: This may have been an adaptation or exaptation for processing plant matter.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the analogy to herbivorous lizards with robust teeth.

claim: Several groups of extant folivorous birds have specialised hindguts to process plant matter.
source: Additionally, several groups of extant folivorous birds have specialised hindguts to process plant matter.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies of avian digestive physiology in the following sentences.

claim: Emus have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods.
source: Both emus (Herd and Dawson, 1984) and geese (Buchsbaum et al., 1986) have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods, and anseriform (Ankney and Afton, 1988; Kehoe et al., 1988) and galliform (Gasaway, 1976; Moss, 1989; Remington, 1989) birds are known to increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets, which allows for a higher percentage to be digested.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Herd and Dawson, 1984.

claim: Geese have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods.
source: Both emus (Herd and Dawson, 1984) and geese (Buchsbaum et al., 1986) have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods, and anseriform (Ankney and Afton, 1988; Kehoe et al., 1988) and galliform (Gasaway, 1976; Moss, 1989; Remington, 1989) birds are known to increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets, which allows for a higher percentage to be digested.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buchsbaum et al., 1986.

claim: Anseriform birds increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets.
source: Both emus (Herd and Dawson, 1984) and geese (Buchsbaum et al., 1986) have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods, and anseriform (Ankney and Afton, 1988; Kehoe et al., 1988) and galliform (Gasaway, 1976; Moss, 1989; Remington, 1989) birds are known to increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets, which allows for a higher percentage to be digested.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ankney and Afton, 1988 and Kehoe et al., 1988.

claim: Galliform birds increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets.
source: Both emus (Herd and Dawson, 1984) and geese (Buchsbaum et al., 1986) have regions of their digestive tract specialised in fermenting fibrous foods, and anseriform (Ankney and Afton, 1988; Kehoe et al., 1988) and galliform (Gasaway, 1976; Moss, 1989; Remington, 1989) birds are known to increase their intestinal lengths when consuming high-fibre diets, which allows for a higher percentage to be digested.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gasaway, 1976; Moss, 1989; and Remington, 1989.

claim: Structures now recognised as plant propagules have been identified in seven enantiornithine specimens.
source: Structures now recognised as plant propagules (Mayr et al., 2020) have been identified in seven enantiornithine specimens (O'Connor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mayr et al., 2020 and O'Connor et al., 2014.

claim: In figured enantiornithine specimens, plant propagules are preserved in the lowest thoracic or pelvic region.
source: Of these, four specimens are figured (STM 10-45, STM 29-8 [Zheng et al., 2013], STM 10-12 [O'Connor et al., 2014], and STM 11-80 [Wang et al., 2016b]), and in these figured specimens the propagules are preserved either in the lowest thoracic (STM 10-45 and STM 11-80) or pelvic (STM 29-8 and STM 10-12) region.
evidence: This is based on examination of figures in cited publications.

claim: Consumulite preservation is most likely with long gut retention times.
source: As previously noted, consumulite preservation is most likely with long gut retention times (Miller and Pittman, 2021), so preservation of these plant propagules specifically in the region inhabited by the hindgut in life implies a prolonged retention in this area where plant matter could ferment and break down.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller and Pittman, 2021 on taphonomy of gut contents.

claim: Preservation of plant propagules in the hindgut region implies prolonged retention where plant matter could ferment and break down.
source: As previously noted, consumulite preservation is most likely with long gut retention times (Miller and Pittman, 2021), so preservation of these plant propagules specifically in the region inhabited by the hindgut in life implies a prolonged retention in this area where plant matter could ferment and break down.
evidence: This is an inference based on the taphonomy of gut contents and the location of preserved plant material.

claim: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis could have sustained folivory with oral processing of plant matter and/or specialised fermentation in the hindgut despite likely lacking a crop and gizzard.
source: So, despite likely lacking a crop and gizzard, Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis could have sustained folivory with oral processing of plant matter and/or specialised fermentation in the hindgut.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on analogies to herbivorous lizards and birds with hindgut fermentation.

claim: The diagnosis of Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis as herbivorous is based on the relatively high strength and efficiency of their jaws.
source: Alternatively, as noted in the FEA discussion, our diagnosis of Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis as herbivorous is based on the relatively high strength and efficiency of their jaws.
evidence: This summarizes the evidence from FEA and mechanical advantage analyses.

claim: Jaw adaptations in Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis indicate evolutionary pressure for the ability to consume plant material, but not necessarily a regular habit of doing so.
source: These adaptations indicate evolutionary pressure for the ability to consume plant material, but not necessarily a regular habit of doing so.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional morphology data considering alternative ecological scenarios.

claim: Fallback foods are well-documented evolutionary drivers of extant animals' functional morphology.
source: 'Fallback foods', foods avoided during normal feeding but essential to survival when alternatives are unobtainable, are well-documented evolutionary drivers of extant animals' functional morphology (Marshall and Wrangham, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marshall and Wrangham, 2007.

claim: The Jehol climate is believed to have been highly variable and affected by local volcanic activity.
source: The Jehol climate is believed to have been highly variable and affected by local volcanic activity (Xu et al., 2020), so specialised herbivory may have been restricted to times when this instability limited other food resources.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Xu et al., 2020 on Jehol paleoclimate.

claim: Specialised herbivory in Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis may have been restricted to times when climate instability limited other food resources.
source: The Jehol climate is believed to have been highly variable and affected by local volcanic activity (Xu et al., 2020), so specialised herbivory may have been restricted to times when this instability limited other food resources.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the variable Jehol climate and the concept of fallback foods.

claim: If herbivory in Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis was restricted to resource scarcity, specialised oral or hindgut processing may not have been necessary.
source: If this is the case, then specialised oral or hindgut processing may not have been necessary to allow Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis to survive short-term resource scarcity.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the fallback food hypothesis.

claim: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids.
source: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids (Figure 5), with total evidence pointing to either a frugivorous or generalist lifestyle.
evidence: This is supported by FEA data showing the lowest MWAM strain in Zhouornis.

claim: Total evidence points to Zhouornis having either a frugivorous or generalist lifestyle.
source: Zhouornis has the strongest jaw among bohaiornithids (Figure 5), with total evidence pointing to either a frugivorous or generalist lifestyle.
evidence: This is based on synthesis of FEA, mechanical advantage, and body mass data.

claim: Only frugivores, generalists, husking granivores, and nectarivores inhabit a region of the FEA strain-space where jaw strain is as low and heterogeneous as in Zhouornis.
source: Only frugivores, generalists, husking granivores, and nectarivores inhabit a region of the FEA strain-space where jaw strain is as low and heterogeneous as in Zhouornis.
evidence: This is based on the FEA results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Zhouornis is the largest bohaiornithid with a mean mass estimate of 758 g for the largest specimen.
source: However, Zhouornis is also the largest bohaiornithid (mean estimate 758 g for the largest specimen), and very few extant granivorous or nectarivorous birds reach this size (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on body mass estimates in Table 3.

claim: Very few extant granivorous or nectarivorous birds reach the size of Zhouornis.
source: However, Zhouornis is also the largest bohaiornithid (mean estimate 758 g for the largest specimen), and very few extant granivorous or nectarivorous birds reach this size (Figure 3).
evidence: This is based on the body mass data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Frugivory and generalist feeding are recovered as likely for Zhouornis from mechanical advantage posterior predictions.
source: Frugivory and generalist feeding are also recovered as likely from MA posterior predictions (Table 4), so these two diets are considered most likely for Zhouornis.
evidence: This is based on the FDA results in Table 4.

claim: Zhouornis pedal traditional morphometric results could support either frugivory or generalist feeding.
source: Pedal TM results could support either diet, with talons similar to both raptors taking small prey (potentially useful for a generalist) and non-raptorial perching birds (as expected of a frugivore).
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claim: If Zhouornis was a generalist, it would potentially have an interesting niche overlap with Pengornis.
source: If Zhouornis was indeed a generalist, it would potentially have an interesting niche overlap with that proposed for Pengornis (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on comparison to the diet reconstruction of Pengornis.

claim: Pengornis shows signs of generalist feeding with ability to raptorially take large prey.
source: Pengornis shows signs of generalist feeding with ability to raptorially take large prey.
evidence: This is based on the diet reconstruction in Miller et al., 2023.

claim: Zhouornis' pes more resembles that of raptors taking prey that is small relative to body size.
source: While Zhouornis' pes more resembles that of raptors taking prey that is small relative to body size, Zhouornis' absolute body size is much larger than Pengornis (mean mass estimate 437 g; Serrano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results and body mass comparisons.

claim: Zhouornis' absolute body size is much larger than Pengornis.
source: While Zhouornis' pes more resembles that of raptors taking prey that is small relative to body size, Zhouornis' absolute body size is much larger than Pengornis (mean mass estimate 437 g; Serrano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on body mass estimates from Table 3 and Serrano et al., 2015.

claim: The difference in body size between Zhouornis and Pengornis may represent a different approach to taking advantage of the same prey resources.
source: This may represent a different approach to taking advantage of the same prey resources.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about niche partitioning based on body size differences.

claim: Zhouornis would be capable of macrocarnivory but less suited for it than Pengornis.
source: We predict Zhouornis would be capable of macrocarnivory but less suited for it than Pengornis; the barred owl (Strix varia) has a similar body mass and claw shape to Zhouornis, and while it is capable of taking large prey like grouse and rabbits it preferentially takes mouse-sized prey (Mazur and James, 2021).
evidence: This is a prediction based on analogy to the barred owl.

claim: The barred owl has a similar body mass and claw shape to Zhouornis.
source: We predict Zhouornis would be capable of macrocarnivory but less suited for it than Pengornis; the barred owl (Strix varia) has a similar body mass and claw shape to Zhouornis, and while it is capable of taking large prey like grouse and rabbits it preferentially takes mouse-sized prey (Mazur and James, 2021).
evidence: This is based on comparison of body mass and pedal TM data.

claim: The barred owl is capable of taking large prey like grouse and rabbits but preferentially takes mouse-sized prey.
source: We predict Zhouornis would be capable of macrocarnivory but less suited for it than Pengornis; the barred owl (Strix varia) has a similar body mass and claw shape to Zhouornis, and while it is capable of taking large prey like grouse and rabbits it preferentially takes mouse-sized prey (Mazur and James, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mazur and James, 2021.

claim: Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis have less clear dietary diagnoses than other bohaiornithids.
source: Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis have less clear diagnoses.
evidence: This is based on the ambiguous results from multiple lines of evidence discussed in the text.

claim: Piscivory and generalist feeding are recovered as likely for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis.
source: Piscivory and generalist feeding are recovered as likely for all three, with folivory also likely for Shenqiornis and Sulcavis.
evidence: This is based on mechanical advantage and FEA results.

claim: Folivory is also likely for Shenqiornis and Sulcavis.
source: Piscivory and generalist feeding are recovered as likely for all three, with folivory also likely for Shenqiornis and Sulcavis.
evidence: This is based on mechanical advantage results and sensitivity analysis of quadrate position.

claim: FEA gives little useful data for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis, with these taxa having intermediate MWAM strains when loaded.
source: Much of the uncertainty stems from FEA giving little useful data, with these taxa having intermediate MWAM strains when loaded (Figure 5) and inhabiting a region of the strain-space shared by most diets (Figure 6A) only ruling out scavenging and tetrapod hunting.
evidence: This is based on the FEA results shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: FEA for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis only rules out scavenging and tetrapod hunting.
source: Much of the uncertainty stems from FEA giving little useful data, with these taxa having intermediate MWAM strains when loaded (Figure 5) and inhabiting a region of the strain-space shared by most diets (Figure 6A) only ruling out scavenging and tetrapod hunting.
evidence: This is based on the FEA results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The intermediate mass of Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis can only rule out granivory, invertivory, and nectarivory.
source: As mentioned above, their intermediate mass can also only rule out granivory, invertivory, and nectarivory.
evidence: This is based on the body mass results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mechanical advantage has poor predictive power in extant birds for discriminating diet in Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis.
source: We are therefore left with MA to discriminate between the remaining diets, which has poor predictive power in extant birds.
evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage results discussed earlier showing overlap between diet groups.

claim: Generalist feeding and piscivory are recovered as somewhat likely for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis from mechanical advantage.
source: Generalist feeding and piscivory are recovered as somewhat likely for all three from MA (Table 4), though as previously proposed this could represent a default prediction (Miller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is based on the FDA results in Table 4.

claim: Folivory cannot be ruled out in Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis due to uncertainty in quadrate placement.
source: Folivory can also not be ruled out in any of these taxa due to uncertainty in quadrate placement (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis of quadrate position.

claim: Pedal traditional morphometrics point to folivory being unlikely in Longusunguis as its talons appear adapted for taking large animal prey.
source: Pedal TM, however, points to folivory being unlikely in Longusunguis as its talons appear adapted for taking large animal prey.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claim: Longusunguis has more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids.
source: Longusunguis notably has more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids (Figures 4 and 6 in Zhou et al., 2021) which is associated with carnivory (Button and Zanno, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2021 and Button and Zanno, 2020.

claim: Recurved teeth are associated with carnivory.
source: Longusunguis notably has more recurved teeth than other bohaiornithids (Figures 4 and 6 in Zhou et al., 2021) which is associated with carnivory (Button and Zanno, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Button and Zanno, 2020.

claim: Skull traditional morphometrics of Longusunguis are most similar to folivorous birds.
source: Skull TM of Longusunguis are most similar to folivorous birds, but given the uncertainty in what developmental constraints are at play we consider folivory overall less likely in Longusunguis than carnivory.
evidence: This is based on the skull TM results in Figure 8.

claim: Folivory is considered overall less likely in Longusunguis than carnivory despite skull morphometrics.
source: Skull TM of Longusunguis are most similar to folivorous birds, but given the uncertainty in what developmental constraints are at play we consider folivory overall less likely in Longusunguis than carnivory.
evidence: This is based on synthesis of multiple lines of evidence, with pedal morphology and tooth shape outweighing skull morphometrics.

claim: Claw shape may point to carnivory in Sulcavis, though its raptorial affinities are questionable.
source: Claw shape may also point to carnivory in Sulcavis, though as discussed above its raptorial affinities are questionable.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results and discussion of Sulcavis' unusual claw morphology.

claim: Shenqiornis only preserves two disarticulated talons.
source: Shenqiornis only preserves two disarticulated talons (Wang et al., 2010), and while these superficially resemble the claws of Zhouornis in size and curvature we cannot quantitatively reject hypotheses of the pes not being adapted for prey capture.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Hypotheses of the pes not being adapted for prey capture cannot be quantitatively rejected for Shenqiornis.
source: Shenqiornis only preserves two disarticulated talons (Wang et al., 2010), and while these superficially resemble the claws of Zhouornis in size and curvature we cannot quantitatively reject hypotheses of the pes not being adapted for prey capture.
evidence: This is based on the limited pedal material available for Shenqiornis.

claim: Hypotheses of folivory in Shenqiornis or Sulcavis cannot be rejected.
source: In turn, we cannot reject hypotheses of folivory in Shenqiornis or Sulcavis (contra our previous carnivorous assignment of Shenqiornis; Miller and Pittman, 2021).
evidence: This is based on the ambiguous evidence from multiple lines of analysis.

claim: Diagnosis of Shenqiornis is complicated by reliance on cf. Sulcavis material to reconstruct its skull.
source: Diagnosis of Shenqiornis is further complicated by the reliance on cf. Sulcavis material to reconstruct its skull (Figure 2D), artificially inflating the functional similarity of the two genera.
evidence: This is based on the skull reconstruction methodology described in the Methods.

claim: Discovery of additional Shenqiornis specimens should clarify the accuracy of the skull reconstruction model.
source: Discovery of additional Shenqiornis specimens should clarify the accuracy of this model.
evidence: This is a prediction about how future fossil discoveries could improve dietary reconstructions.

claim: Investigating additional lines of evidence is necessary for Longusunguis, Shenqiornis, and Sulcavis dietary diagnosis.
source: In any case, even with four lines of evidence the dietary diagnosis of these three taxa remains tentative, and investigating additional lines of evidence (e.g. dental microwear, muscle reconstruction, or stable isotope analysis; Miller and Pittman, 2021) is necessary.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the current study and suggestions for future research.

claim: Beiguornis preserves neither a skull nor talons.
source: Beiguornis preserves neither a skull nor talons (Wang, 2022a), so only mass data is available.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang, 2022a describing the Beiguornis specimen.

claim: Only invertivory, granivory, and nectarivory can be considered unlikely for Beiguornis based on its mass.
source: As with most bohaiornithids, the only diets which can be considered unlikely based on its mass are invertivory, granivory, and nectarivory.
evidence: This is based on the body mass estimate for Beiguornis in Table 3 and the mass-diet relationships in Figure 3.

claim: Further ecological information for Beiguornis will require new techniques or more complete specimens.
source: Further ecological information will require new techniques or more complete specimens.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current data for Beiguornis.

claim: The results support hypotheses of raptorial behaviour in bohaiornithids, though not for every taxon.
source: Our results support hypotheses of raptorial behaviour (Miller and Pittman, 2021; Wang, 2014a; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Li et al., 2014) in bohaiornithids, though not for every taxon.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results showing some taxa with raptorial claw morphology.

claim: Longusunguis is interpreted as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes.
source: We interpret Longusunguis as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes, and Zhouornis as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claim: Zhouornis is interpreted as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
source: We interpret Longusunguis as a small predator adapted to take prey too large to be completely encircled by the pes, and Zhouornis as potentially a large predator whose talons were adapted to take prey which could be fully encircled by the pes.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claim: Sulcavis has a greatly enlarged and recurved digit I but lacks any enlarged opposed digit that could be used to grip.
source: Sulcavis has a greatly enlarged and recurved digit I as expected in a raptor, but lacks any enlarged opposed digit that could be used to grip.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM data and description of Sulcavis morphology.

claim: The unusual claw morphology of Sulcavis could be taphonomy obscuring the full extent of digit II or a different, unaccounted for use of the pes.
source: As noted above, this could be taphonomy obscuring the full extent of digit II or a different, unaccounted for use of the pes.
evidence: This is speculation about alternative explanations for Sulcavis' unusual claw morphology.

claim: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds.
source: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds, and while the talons of Bohaiornis are between those of raptors and non-raptors we interpret them as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results in Figure 7 and Table 6.

claim: The talons of Bohaiornis are interpreted as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
source: The talons of Parabohaiornis are most akin to non-raptorial perching birds, and while the talons of Bohaiornis are between those of raptors and non-raptors we interpret them as non-raptorial given the taxon's herbivorous skull adaptations.
evidence: This is based on synthesis of pedal TM and jaw functional morphology data.

claim: The alleged rangle in Bohaiornis has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth.
source: Note that the alleged rangle (raptorial gastroliths) used as previous evidence of raptorial behaviour in Bohaiornis (Li et al., 2014) has been reinterpreted as postmortem mineral growth (Liu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2014 and Liu et al., 2021.

claim: Specimens of Shenqiornis preserving talons are needed to opine on whether it was adapted for raptorial behaviour.
source: Specimens of Shenqiornis preserving talons are needed to opine on whether it was adapted for raptorial behaviour.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current fossil material.

claim: The study supports hypotheses of durophagy in bohaiornithids, though with the caveat that their adaptations are less extreme than what one usually considers an avian durophage.
source: We also support hypotheses of durophagy (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a; O'Connor et al., 2013; Chiappe and Meng, 2016; Zhou et al., 2021) in bohaiornithids, though with the caveat that their adaptations are less extreme than what one usually considers an avian durophage.
evidence: This is based on comparison of bohaiornithid jaw mechanics and strength to extant durophagous birds.

claim: The first proposal of durophagy in a bohaiornithid was made in contrast to proposing most other enantiornithines as general insectivores limited to small arthropods with softer cuticles.
source: The first proposal of durophagy in a bohaiornithid is made in contrast to proposing most other enantiornithines as 'general insectivore[s], limited to small arthropods with softer cuticles' (O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor and Chiappe, 2011a.

claim: Bohaiornithids are durophagous in the sense that they have higher jaw strengths than other modelled enantiornithines.
source: We support Bohaiornithids as durophagous in the sense that they have higher jaw strengths than other modelled enantiornithines (see above).
evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA results between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithine families.

claim: Bohaiornithids appear adapted for taking foods harder and tougher than soft-bodied arthropods.
source: They appear adapted for taking foods harder and tougher than soft-bodied arthropods, but the same could be said for pengornithids.
evidence: This is based on the FEA and mechanical advantage results.

claim: In living birds, 'durophagy' typically refers to cracking hard foods like seeds or nuts within the beak.
source: In living birds, 'durophagy' typically refers to cracking hard foods like seeds or nuts within the beak (Soons et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soons et al., 2010 defining durophagy in birds.

claim: Bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw.
source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage and FEA results comparing bohaiornithids to extant durophagous birds.

claim: Bohaiornithids lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores.
source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage results showing lower MA values in bohaiornithids than in husking granivores.

claim: Bohaiornithids fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
source: As examined in the MA and FEA discussion sections, bohaiornithids resemble extant husking granivores in both the relative height of their upper jaw and the overall strain under loading of their lower jaw; however, they lack the adaptations for bite force production of husking granivores and fall short of parrots in all potential durophagy metrics.
evidence: This is based on comparison of mechanical advantage and FEA results between bohaiornithids and parrots.

claim: Bohaiornithids do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
source: Bohaiornithids, therefore, do not display adaptations for taking foods as hard as extant birds commonly considered durophages.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison to extant durophagous birds.

claim: Bohaiornithid tooth shape tightly clusters in phylomorphospace analyses.
source: Bohaiornithid tooth shape does tightly cluster in the study's phylomorphospaces (Figures 4–6 in Zhou et al., 2021), but they notably tend to take a central position in the morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
evidence: This is based on examination of figures in Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: Bohaiornithids tend to take a central position in tooth shape morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
source: Bohaiornithid tooth shape does tightly cluster in the study's phylomorphospaces (Figures 4–6 in Zhou et al., 2021), but they notably tend to take a central position in the morphospace and overlap with purported granivores, insectivores, and piscivores.
evidence: This is based on examination of figures in Zhou et al., 2021.

claim: The similarity in bohaiornithid tooth shape is suggested to be driven by phylogeny rather than diet.
source: Given this overlap and the ecological diversity within the group we support here, we suggest the similarity in bohaiornithid tooth shape is driven by phylogeny rather than, as proposed by Zhou et al., 2021, diet.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dietary diversity found in this study contrasted with the morphological similarity in tooth shape.

claim: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively rather than adaptations to a specialised diet shared across the clade.
source: The robust teeth in Bohaiornithidae may serve as general-use tools capable of processing diverse foods effectively rather than adaptations to a specialised diet shared across the clade.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the functional significance of bohaiornithid tooth morphology based on the dietary diversity found in the study.

claim: Bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families.
source: Our data suggest that bohaiornithids cover a greater ecological breadth than previously studied enantiornithine families (Figure 9).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the dietary diversity found in bohaiornithids to that in longipterygids and pengornithids.

claim: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment.
source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2022.

claim: The mass results in this study suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected.
source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is based on the refined body mass data and cut-offs presented in this study.

claim: Pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet.
source: Longipterygids are reconstructed as mainly invertivorous with variability in foraging environment (Miller et al., 2022; Figure 1, left; though our mass results here suggest the hypothesis of Longipteryx as a piscivore cannot be rejected, contra Miller et al., 2022, see Body Mass Discussion), and pengornithids are reconstructed as generally piscivorous with Pengornis diversifying into a more generalist and macrocarnivorous diet (Miller et al., 2023; Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2023.

claim: Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores.
source: In contrast, Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores while Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
evidence: This is based on the mechanical advantage, FEA, and body mass results.

claim: Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
source: In contrast, Bohaiornis and Parabohaiornis show adaptations reminiscent of extant herbivores while Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis were adapted for taking vertebrate prey.
evidence: This is based on the pedal TM results and other lines of evidence.

claim: The differences in the mass and talon shape of Longusunguis and Zhouornis imply partitioning of the carnivorous niche.
source: The differences in the mass and talon shape of the latter pair further imply partitioning of the carnivorous niche.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differences in body size and claw morphology between these two taxa.

claim: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.
source: The increased dietary breadth in Bohaiornithidae appears to stem from increased strength in the bohaiornithid skull.
evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA results between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithine families.

claim: Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae.
source: In particular, Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae, which is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines (Wang et al., 2021b), and from the ancestral enantiornithine skull (Table 7).
evidence: This is based on comparison of jaw strength and ancestral state reconstructions.

claim: Pengornithid skull architecture is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines.
source: In particular, Longipterygidae and Bohaiornithidae may represent opposite evolutionary trajectories from the skull architecture of Pengornithidae, which is considered plesiomorphic for enantiornithines (Wang et al., 2021b), and from the ancestral enantiornithine skull (Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021b.

claim: Bohaiornithid skulls and teeth have been qualitatively described as robust in past works.
source: Past works (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe et al., 2019) have qualitatively described bohaiornithid skulls and teeth as robust, though when using ACH to quantify robusticity bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang, 2014a and Chiappe et al., 2019.

claim: When using ACH to quantify robusticity, bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
source: Past works (Wang, 2014a; Chiappe et al., 2019) have qualitatively described bohaiornithid skulls and teeth as robust, though when using ACH to quantify robusticity bohaiornithids are not particularly remarkable.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values between bohaiornithids and other enantiornithines.

claim: There is a large difference in ACH between longipterygids and pengornithids.
source: While there is a large difference between longipterygids (ACH 0.09–0.11, x̄ = 0.10; Miller et al., 2022) and pengornithids (ACH 0.22–0.23, x̄ = 0.23; Miller et al., 2023), bohaiornithid skulls (ACH 0.21–0.26, x̄ = 0.24) are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values from this study and previous studies.

claim: Bohaiornithid skulls are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids based on ACH.
source: While there is a large difference between longipterygids (ACH 0.09–0.11, x̄ = 0.10; Miller et al., 2022) and pengornithids (ACH 0.22–0.23, x̄ = 0.23; Miller et al., 2023), bohaiornithid skulls (ACH 0.21–0.26, x̄ = 0.24) are only slightly more robust than those of pengornithids.
evidence: This is based on comparison of ACH values.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae converged upon their level of robusticity from an ancestor whose ACH was between them and Longipterygidae.
source: Ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 9—figure supplement 3K) predicts Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae converged upon this level of robusticity from an ancestor whose ACH was between them and Longipterygidae.
evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: There is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families.
source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
evidence: This is based on comparison of FEA MWAM strain values between the three families.

claim: Longipterygids have the weakest jaws among Jehol enantiornithine families.
source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
evidence: This is based on FEA results from Miller et al., 2022.

claim: Pengornithid jaws are stronger than longipterygid jaws.
source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
evidence: This is based on FEA results from Miller et al., 2023.

claim: Bohaiornithid jaws are stronger than pengornithid jaws.
source: What we find more noteworthy than robusticity is a distinct stepwise increase in jaw strength between Jehol enantiornithine families: longipterygids have the weakest jaws (259–345 µε, x̄ = 309 µε; Miller et al., 2022), with pengornithid jaws stronger (190–275 µε, x̄ = 222 µε; Miller et al., 2023), and bohaiornithids' stronger still (89–156 µε, x̄ = 128 µε).
evidence: This is based on FEA results from this study.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction supports bohaiornithids and longipterygids diversifying from a common ancestor with pengornithid-like jaw strength.
source: Ancestral state reconstruction supports bohaiornithids and longipterygids diversifying from a common ancestor with pengornithid-like jaw strength (Figure 9—figure supplement 3), though a lack of jaw strength data from families outside these three limits the reliability of this reconstruction.
evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results, with acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: An increase in jaw strength may have allowed Bohaiornithidae to process a wider variety of difficult-to-process foods than contemporary groups and ecologically diversify.
source: An increase in jaw strength may have allowed Bohaiornithidae to process a wider variety of difficult-to-process foods than contemporary groups and ecologically diversify, but the poor resolution of relationships within and near the clade (Wang et al., 2021b; Li et al., 2022; Table 1) makes this possibility difficult to test.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary significance of increased jaw strength, with acknowledgment of phylogenetic uncertainty.

claim: The skull of Fortunguavis appears to have a robust surangular and pterygoid.
source: For instance, the skull of Fortunguavis, while overall poorly preserved, does appear to have a robust surangular and pterygoid (Wang et al., 2014b) and is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2014b.

claim: Fortunguavis is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
source: For instance, the skull of Fortunguavis, while overall poorly preserved, does appear to have a robust surangular and pterygoid (Wang et al., 2014b) and is commonly recovered as sister to Bohaiornithidae.
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic summary in Table 1.

claim: Strengthening of the skull may be present in more 'bohaiornithid-like' enantiornithines and even convergent between them.
source: Strengthening of the skull may therefore be present in more 'bohaiornithid-like' enantiornithines (sensu Wang et al., 2022b) and even convergent between them.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the robust skull elements in Fortunguavis and phylogenetic relationships.

claim: Shenqiornis is the geologically oldest bohaiornithid.
source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
evidence: This is based on the dating of the Qiaotou Formation described in the Methods.

claim: Shenqiornis has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids.
source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
evidence: This is based on the FEA results in Figure 5.

claim: The skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
source: Shenqiornis, the geologically oldest bohaiornithid, has a jaw strength intermediate within bohaiornithids (Figure 5) which does imply the skull strengthening adaptations in Bohaiornithidae at least predate 124 Ma.
evidence: This is an inference based on the age of Shenqiornis and its jaw strength.

claim: Longipterygids were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources.
source: Longipterygids, conversely, were limited by their weak and gracile jaws to relatively soft and compliant food sources (Miller et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2022.

claim: Whether the gracile jaws of longipterygids were adaptations to specialise in soft and compliant prey, or had unrelated benefits and coincidentally constrained their diet, remains unclear.
source: However, whether the gracile jaws of longipterygids were adaptations to specialise in soft and compliant prey, or had unrelated benefits and coincidentally constrained their diet, remains unclear.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of uncertainty about the evolutionary drivers of longipterygid jaw morphology.

claim: Bohaiornithids and Pengornithids are notably larger than other Jehol enantiornithines.
source: Bohaiornithids and Pengornithids are notably larger than other Jehol enantiornithines (Miller and Pittman, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller and Pittman, 2021.

claim: Only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis are interpreted as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids among bohaiornithids.
source: While we interpret only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids, this size increase does make invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
evidence: This is based on the dietary reconstructions from this study.

claim: The size increase in bohaiornithids and pengornithids makes invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
source: While we interpret only Longusunguis and possibly Zhouornis as inhabiting similar niches to pengornithids, this size increase does make invertivory unlikely in every pengornithid and bohaiornithid.
evidence: This is based on the body mass results and mass-diet relationships.

claim: The food web of the Jehol Biota is generally understood to be dominated by small animals.
source: The food web of the Jehol Biota is generally understood to be dominated by small animals (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b), particularly in the Jiufotang formation in which bohaiornithids and pengornithids are most diverse.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsukawa et al., 2014 and O'Connor et al., 2019b.

claim: Interspecific competition for invertebrates would be expected to be high in the Jehol ecosystem.
source: Accordingly, one would expect interspecific competition for invertebrates to be high in this ecosystem.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the dominance of small animals in the Jehol food web.

claim: Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae may be lineages which attempted to alleviate invertivorous competition by diversifying into consuming vertebrate or plant prey.
source: Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae (alongside the ornithurine family Songlingornithidae; Miller and Pittman, 2021), then, may be lineages which attempted to alleviate invertivorous competition by diversifying into consuming vertebrate or plant prey.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of dietary diversification in these families.

claim: Size increase in bohaiornithids and pengornithids is also commonly interpreted as defence against predation.
source: Alternatively, size increase is also commonly interpreted as defence against predation.
evidence: This is a statement of a common interpretation in evolutionary biology.

claim: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines.
source: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines (O'Connor et al., 2011b) and the Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Connor et al., 2011b documenting predation on enantiornithines.

claim: The Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor.
source: Microraptor was definitely capable of preying on smaller enantiornithines (O'Connor et al., 2011b) and the Jehol Biota had many carnivores larger than Microraptor (Matsukawa et al., 2014; O'Connor et al., 2019b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Matsukawa et al., 2014 and O'Connor et al., 2019b.

claim: The more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation may have provided pressure to grow larger when bohaiornithids and pengornithids first emerged.
source: These possibilities need not be mutually exclusive: the more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have provided pressure to grow larger when these clades first emerged, and the subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have allowed them to further diversify.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of body size increase, supported by citation to Matsukawa et al., 2014.

claim: The subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation may have allowed bohaiornithids and pengornithids to further diversify.
source: These possibilities need not be mutually exclusive: the more abundant large carnivores in the Yixian formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have provided pressure to grow larger when these clades first emerged, and the subsequent reduction in large carnivores by the Jiufotang formation (Matsukawa et al., 2014) may have allowed them to further diversify.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the evolutionary drivers of dietary diversification, supported by citation to Matsukawa et al., 2014.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
source: Indeed, ancestral state reconstruction (Figure 9—figure supplement 1) predicts a concurrent increase in body mass for Bohaiornithidae and Pengornithidae near 125 Ma.
evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: Ancestral state reconstruction recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
source: Interestingly, though, it recovers the large mass of pengornithids as convergent, not present ancestrally in the clade.
evidence: This is based on the ancestral state reconstruction results.

claim: The convergent large mass in pengornithids is driven by the earliest pengornithid, Eopengornis, being smaller than its more recent relatives.
source: This is driven by the earliest pengornithid, Eopengornis, being smaller than its more recent relatives.
evidence: This is based on body mass estimates for Eopengornis compared to other pengornithids.

claim: No bohaiornithid is known from the same time frame as Eopengornis.
source: No bohaiornithid is known from this time frame, so we cannot yet comment on if their increased body mass is similarly convergent or ancestral to Bohaiornithidae as a whole.
evidence: This is based on the fossil record and dating of bohaiornithid specimens.

claim: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g.
source: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Table 7), pointing to frugivory or generalist feeding.
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of body mass.

claim: The body mass of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes points to frugivory or generalist feeding.
source: The common ancestor of Enantiornithes likely had a body mass near 200 g (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, Table 7), pointing to frugivory or generalist feeding.
evidence: This is based on the mass-diet relationships established in this study.

claim: The mechanical advantage and jaw robusticity of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes was likely intermediate to low.
source: Its MA and jaw robusticity was likely intermediate to low (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), overall resembling extant generalists, piscivores, and invertivores (Table 8).
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of mechanical advantage.

claim: The mechanical advantage of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes overall resembles extant generalists, piscivores, and invertivores.
source: Its MA and jaw robusticity was likely intermediate to low (Figure 9—figure supplement 2), overall resembling extant generalists, piscivores, and invertivores (Table 8).
evidence: This is based on FDA posterior probabilities in Table 8.

claim: The jaw strain during a bite of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes is estimated at 227 µε.
source: Its jaw strain during a bite is estimated at 227 µε (Table 7), within the range of Pengornithidae (Figure 9—figure supplement 3) and thus consistent with folivory, swallowing granivory, generalist feeding, and invertivory (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of FEA MWAM strain.

claim: The jaw strain of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes is within the range of Pengornithidae.
source: Its jaw strain during a bite is estimated at 227 µε (Table 7), within the range of Pengornithidae (Figure 9—figure supplement 3) and thus consistent with folivory, swallowing granivory, generalist feeding, and invertivory (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on comparison to pengornithid FEA results.

claim: The jaw strain of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes is consistent with folivory, swallowing granivory, generalist feeding, and invertivory.
source: Its jaw strain during a bite is estimated at 227 µε (Table 7), within the range of Pengornithidae (Figure 9—figure supplement 3) and thus consistent with folivory, swallowing granivory, generalist feeding, and invertivory (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on the FEA-diet relationships established in Miller et al., 2023.

claim: The claws of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes are shaped in a way that is dissimilar from any extant bird included in this study.
source: The claws of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes are shaped in a way that is dissimilar from any extant bird included in this study, plotting between non-raptorial perchers and shrikes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on ancestral state reconstruction of pedal TM plotted in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The claw shape of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes is reminiscent of Eopengornis.
source: This is reminiscent of Eopengornis, and this claw shape has been interpreted as arboreal and allowing for very limited prey manipulation (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is based on comparison to Eopengornis and citation to Miller et al., 2023.

claim: The claw shape of the common ancestor of Enantiornithes has been interpreted as arboreal and allowing for very limited prey manipulation.
source: This is reminiscent of Eopengornis, and this claw shape has been interpreted as arboreal and allowing for very limited prey manipulation (Miller et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2023.

claim: The lines of evidence point to the common ancestor of Enantiornithes being an arboreal generalist feeder.
source: Overall, these lines of evidence point to the common ancestor of Enantiornithes being an arboreal generalist feeder.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the ancestral state reconstructions from multiple lines of evidence.

claim: If the common ancestor of Enantiornithes was an arboreal generalist feeder, the numerous ecological specialisations seen within Enantiornithes likely represent lineages already exploiting a resource further specialising in it.
source: If this is the case, then the numerous ecological specialisations seen within Enantiornithes likely represent lineages already exploiting a resource further specialising in it, rather than dramatic trophic shifts.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the pattern of dietary evolution in enantiornithines.

claim: One enantiornithine lineage, that leading to both Longipterygidae and Eoalulavis, appears to be ancestrally invertivorous.
source: One enantiornithine lineage, that leading to both Longipterygidae and Eoalulavis, does appear to be ancestrally invertivorous (Figure 9).
